publicTrace: Base rate / reference class: The post-expanded-CTC SPM child poverty series (2021–2024) has averaged approximately 13.2 pct, with the 2024 print at 13.4 pct and a recent year-over-year change of −0.3 pct. The 2009–2019 pre-expansion average was roughly 15–18 pct, so the post-2021 regime is the relevant reference class.

Point estimate mechanism: A weighted blend of the PolicyEngine current-law microsimulation prior (13.0 pct, weight 0.55), the post-expansion Census SPM history (13.2 pct, weight 0.35), and the latest published 2024 print (13.4 pct, weight 0.10), minus a small macro adjustment (−0.05 pct), yields a calibrated point estimate of approximately 13.0 pct.

Uncertainty widening: The 80% interval is set at roughly 11.2–14.5 pct (lower half-width ~1.8 pct, upper half-width ~1.5 pct), reflecting ASEC sampling variance (~0.3–0.5 pct), SPM resource/expense volatility (MOOP, housing adjustments), and policy uncertainty around SNAP, EITC, and CTC phase-in rules for 2025.

Disconfirming consideration (upside risk): If SNAP benefit reductions, Medicaid unwinding, or housing cost increases materially raise out-of-pocket burdens in 2025, the SPM rate could exceed 14.5 pct, placing the outcome above the 80% interval upper bound.

Disconfirming consideration (downside risk): If labor market strength, real wage gains, or expanded state-level EITC/CTC supplements reduce child poverty faster than the current-law baseline implies, the rate could fall below 11.2 pct.

Data availability caveat: The Census SPM tables page was fetched live but the child-poverty history is a prototype seed; no machine-readable SPM table endpoint was parsed. The PolicyEngine check confirms current-law status but is not a fresh microsimulation run. Both inputs are treated as informative priors, not ground truth, and uncertainty is widened accordingly.

The distribution is intentionally left-skewed relative to a symmetric normal: the lower tail is heavier because the post-2021 regime has shown persistent downward pressure from expanded transfers, while the upper tail reflects policy rollback and macro shock risks.
assumptions: Current-law policy (no major CTC, SNAP, or EITC legislative changes enacted for 2025) holds throughout the calendar year, consistent with the PolicyEngine current-law check.
The post-2021 SPM child poverty regime (average ~13.2 pct) is the relevant reference class; pre-2021 prints above 15 pct are treated as a structurally different policy environment.
ASEC sampling and SPM methodology remain unchanged from the 2024 release; no methodological revision is assumed.
Macro conditions (unemployment, real wages, inflation) evolve in line with CBO/Fed baseline projections for 2025, with no severe recession or boom.
dataCaveats: The SPM child-poverty history used here is a prototype seed value, not a machine-parsed Census SPM table; the 2024 print of 13.4 pct and post-expansion average of 13.2 pct are treated as informative but not verified against the live Census data table endpoint.

The PolicyEngine prior of 13.0 pct reflects a stored current-law estimate, not a fresh server-side microsimulation for calendar year 2025; it may not capture mid-year regulatory changes or updated tax parameters.

SPM estimates are sensitive to geographic housing cost adjustments and MOOP imputations, which can shift the series by 0.3–0.8 pct independently of policy changes, adding model uncertainty beyond sampling variance.

The Census release schedule page confirms a September 2026 release for 2025 data, but the exact publication date and any methodological notes are not yet available, introducing timing and revision risk.
drivers: SNAP benefit levels and participation rates among families with children
Child Tax Credit and EITC refundability rules under current law
Medical out-of-pocket expense burdens (MOOP) affecting SPM resource net
Real wage growth and employment rates for parents of young children
Geographic housing cost adjustments embedded in SPM thresholds
